extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and strategic advisors considering forum/venue selection for multinational patent litigation
extracted.subtask_short: venue selection for global patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and practical criteria for choosing and litigating patents in national courts (UK, France, Netherlands examples), covering remedies, interim relief, costs, fees recovery, revocation/defenses, and jurisdiction-specific procedures and strategic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim injunction test (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a serious question to be tried?; where does the balance of convenience lie (including a consideration of whether damages would be an adequate remedy)?; are there any special factors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For interim injunctions in practice (largely in pharma/generics), the patentee must apply without delay and provide a cross-undertaking as to damages payable if injunction is wrongly granted. Cross-undertakings can also be in favor of third parties. Interim injunctions are rare outside these contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for prompt interim injunction application (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a patentee to be successful, the interim injunction application must be made without delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay can defeat the application; a cross-undertaking as to damages is required and can cover third parties suffering loss from the injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-undertaking as to damages (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must give a cross-undertaking as to the damages that will be payable to the defendant if the injunction is later deemed wrongly granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-undertakings can also be extended to third parties; this is a standard safeguard in interim relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final injunctions — grant and limits (UK/France)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final injunction may be granted following a substantive trial to mandate or prevent acts (manufacture, sale, importation) and may be stayed pending appeal; a final injunction may not be granted if the cost of design-around is disproportionate or if the licence demanded is excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the ordinary course, a final injunction will be granted following a finding of infringement, but proportionality and fairness considerations (design-around cost, excessive licences) can preclude it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Springboard injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions that continue post-patent expiry may be available where the final product is not infringing but was developed using infringing acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any such injunction should reflect the advantage gained by the infringing use and must not put the patentee in a better position than if there had been no infringement. These remedies are extremely rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery up or destruction of infringing goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Where goods are found to infringe, courts may order delivery up or destruction of any patented product or any article in which that product is inextricably comprised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available at the request of the applicant as a standard form of injunctive/ancillary relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages versus account of profits — election timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may seek damages or an account of profits; both remedies are usually claimed in the alternative in the particulars of claim and the election is made only after infringement has been found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim both alternatives; election occurs post-determination of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — compensatory principle and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, damages are compensatory, not punitive. If the patentee sells/manufactures products, it may claim lost sales and ancillary item losses; if the patentee licenses the patent, damages are usually a royalty rate based on comparable licences; where the patentee neither manufactures nor licenses, the court will determine a notional royalty applying the user principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general rule is to put the injured party in the same position it would have been in but for the wrong. The burden of proof lies with the claimant but damages are assessed liberally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits — approach
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of profits is rare; the court will assess overall profit and then make an apportionment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically less favorable to claimants than damages inquiries; used when unjust enrichment measurement is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND license determination (UK Supreme Court holding)
rubrics_metrics.description: UK courts have jurisdiction to grant an injunction in respect of a UK SEP unless the implementer enters into a FRAND licence; such a FRAND licence may be a global licence of a multinational portfolio; the UK Court may determine the terms of that licence without both parties' agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision makes English courts a leading forum for resolving global SEP-FRAND disputes and affects venue choice for SEP owners and implementers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor — Cost of litigation (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the UK is relatively expensive, costs are generally lower than in the U.S.; options include issuing in IPEC or using the Shorter Trials Scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPEC is for smaller, shorter, less complex, lower value actions with a cap on financial remedies (£500,000 unless agreed otherwise) and fixed costs recovery; Shorter Trials Scheme lists trials more quickly and aims for judgment within six weeks of trial but suits less complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPEC characteristics (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Intellectual Property Enterprise Court is a specialist IP court with streamlined procedure, fixed costs recovery, and a cap of £500,000 on financial remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed for SMEs and lower-value actions; popular forum for those aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter Trials Scheme (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enables parties to resolve disputes in a shorter time period, with trials listed more quickly and judgment within six weeks of trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate only for less complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of fees — loser pays and judicial discretion (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: General principle: the unsuccessful party is ordered to pay the costs of the successful party; the court has wide discretion and considers conduct, partial success, complexity, settlement/mediation attempts, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee shifting is often issue-based; assessment determines reasonable and proportionate amounts; indemnity costs are less common and penal in nature; court resolves doubt in favor of receiving party when indemnity costs apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs assessment and proportionality (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once recoverability is determined, a separate 'assessment' process determines the amount recoverable according to what was reasonably and proportionately incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party seeking recovery must prove reasonableness and proportionality. IPEC has caps/limits on recoverable costs per stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of contested validity (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee successful in upholding its patent should seek a certificate of contested validity; where granted, in subsequent proceedings the patentee is entitled to be awarded costs as between solicitor and own client (subject to court discretion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such costs are generally more generous than standard or indemnity costs; court has discretion whether to grant certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation grounds (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under UK law, five grounds for revocation by a third party: Nonpatentability (not novel/inventive or excluded subject-matter), Nonentitlement, Insufficiency (specification doesn't enable skilled person), Added matter (subject-matter extends beyond originally filed content), Unallowable post-grant extension (impermissible amendment after grant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No standing required to bring a revocation claim in the UK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaratory relief (UK) — scope and Arrow declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provision allows declarations of noninfringement by any party; courts have broad inherent jurisdiction to make declarations that serve a useful purpose. Arrow declarations can confirm that an applicant's product/process was known or obvious at a relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrow declarations are used when divisional applications or shielding subject matter threaten the applicant; successful declaration provides a defence to future infringement claims because claims cannot be both valid and infringed if product/process was known or obvious at priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaratory relief — SPCs and nonessentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: English courts can grant declaratory relief concerning Supplementary Protection Certificates (SPCs) that have yet to be granted, and declarations of nonessentiality (that a patent is not essential to a standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPC declarations may be sought on basis that any SPC application by the patentee would be invalid; courts may grant declarations of noninfringement of European patents in other jurisdictions provided validity is not in issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groundless threats test (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged infringer may bring an action for groundless threats; the 'threat' is actionable if it is a 'threat of infringement proceedings' following an objective two-step test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats need not be limited to UK proceedings nor directed at a particular individual. There is a safe harbor for communications for 'permitted purposes' (notifying existence of patent, discovering whether/by whom patent is infringed, giving notice that a person has a right under a patent where awareness is relevant).

rubrics_metrics.name: France — availability of injunctions and combined validity/infringement adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: France enables obtaining an injunction in a major EU market where validity and infringement are adjudicated at the same time by the same specialized judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a key reason to commence proceedings in France for multinational strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and seizure (saisie-contrefaçon) mechanism (France)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte search-and-seizure orders allow a bailiff to enter defendant premises, describe accused product/process, seize samples and take copies of documentation evidencing materiality/origin/scope of infringement; claimant has 31 days to launch proceedings or the seizure is void and materials returned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No discovery/disclosure in French system, so this measure is heavily used (performed in >80% of infringement proceedings) and evidence obtained can often be used in other jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings and expert use in France
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings before civil courts are predominantly written; oral hearings are usually short (half day per patent or more if necessary). Use of experts is extremely rare; where used they prepare written reports and are not typically examined or cross-examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can file expert reports prepared for foreign proceedings; written pleadings and exhibits carry substantial weight with judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: France — time to trial and relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary proceedings typically take 2–4 months (3–6 months if appealed) and can be shortened for urgency; main first-instance proceedings with counterclaim for invalidity last 18–24 months (12–18 months if only infringement or invalidity); appeals usually decided in ~2 years and are heard de novo; decisions are immediately enforceable even if appealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages often pursued in a second phase after liability judgment, lasting less than a year; advance on damages can be awarded even in preliminary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: France — likelihood of prevailing (statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paris courts are seen as patent-friendly: patents are invalidated in about one-third of cases, held valid but not infringed in about one-third, and held valid and infringed in about one-third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These historical averages inform expectations about plaintiff success rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: France — availability of relief in preliminary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunction proceedings consider both validity and infringement on short timeframes; to obtain a preliminary injunction, validity and infringement should not be seriously challengeable; proportionality may lead judges to refrain, but this is seldom applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents surviving opposition or successfully litigated elsewhere have higher chances; advance on damages can accompany preliminary injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: France — cost of litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: France is generally reasonable compared to common-law systems; there are no court fees and costs are limited to attorneys' fees. First-instance costs where both validity and infringement are at stake usually range between €150,000 and €500,000 depending on complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs may be higher for high-stakes cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: France — recovery of fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The winning party can claim reimbursement of attorneys' fees, but the grant and amount are within the court's discretion; usually the amount awarded ranges between 20% and 70% of attorneys' fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed statutory rule for determining amounts; discretion leads to variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: France — defendant-initiated relief options
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants can initiate invalidity actions where they show an interest; grounds include lack of novelty, inventive step, industrial application, insufficiency, added matter, or undue extension. Declaratory noninfringement actions proceed in two phases: an amicable phase inviting the patentee's opinion, then a judicial phase by summons if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FRAND-specific contractual breach claims (breach of ETSI declaration) have been recognized by French courts; procedural prerequisites (amicable step) apply for noninfringement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: France — anti-anti-suit injunctions and preliminary injunction trends
rubrics_metrics.description: French courts have ordered anti-anti-suit injunctions in SEP contexts where non-European anti-suit injunctions threatened the patentee's right to litigate French patents; success rates of preliminary injunctions have increased in recent years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may find anti-anti-suit injunctions admissible when needed to protect litigation rights in France; preliminary injunction thresholds have arguably lowered (serious doubts standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Netherlands — market and jurisdictional reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The Netherlands hosts headquarters and distribution hubs for many multinationals; presence of a Dutch subsidiary is generally sufficient for Dutch courts to assume jurisdiction over foreign parents and grant relief against subsidiaries and foreign parent companies, potentially cross-border.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This jurisdictional reach and economic profile make the Netherlands attractive for international patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Netherlands — quality of adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent litigation is concentrated in The Hague before specialized courts with experienced judges (often with technical backgrounds), leading to excellent quality and predictable adjudication. The judiciary is independent and not perceived as biased against NPEs or foreign litigants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dutch courts are used to EPO case law (problem-solution approach) and treat foreign decisions as persuasive; they decide cases based on briefs, exhibits, and a typically short final hearing without live expert cross-examination, but meaningful expert involvement through written declarations and informal court questioning is possible. Foreign experts and English-language handling are routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Netherlands — procedural/evidence features
rubrics_metrics.description: Dutch procedural law provides options to retrieve evidence from opposing parties or third parties; the amount of evidence required depends on the level of substantiation by the defendant—if a plaintiff can make infringement sufficiently plausible, courts will usually allow further evidence-gathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: plaintiffs who can make initial plausibility may obtain means to gather evidence to prove the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO problem-solution approach usage (Netherlands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dutch courts apply established EPO case law, most importantly the problem-solution approach for assessing inventive step: determine closest prior art, establish objective technical problem, and consider if the claimed invention would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO decisions are persuasive and often relied upon by Dutch courts when assessing validity.
